opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the hardware story is underrated in how much it changes the picture. Not that long ago, a capable humanoid was something only a handful of well-funded labs could afford. These were bespoke machines, often several hundred thousand dollars each, and fragile enough that you were nervous every time you ran an experiment. That shapes the whole research culture. If your robot is that expensive, you can't afford to let it fail, and if you can't let it fail, you can't learn from it at scale.

Now we're seeing humanoids, and very capable ones, coming in at a fraction of that, roughly the price of a car or less depending on the platform. That changes everything downstream. A university lab can buy a few. A startup can buy a fleet. And once lots of people have the hardware, you get many more experiments, much more data, and many more people iterating on the software stack. That's how computing has always moved: cheap, widely available hardware is what lets the ecosystem explode.

The second reason I'm optimistic is data. Robotics has never had its "internet," the giant pile of training data that made language models possible. You can't scrape motor control from the web. You have to collect it through teleoperation, from robots acting in the world, or synthesize it in simulation. Cheaper robots mean more robots deployed, which means more real-world data, and that feeds back into better models. Combine that with simulation, where we can generate effectively unlimited experience on GPUs, and you start to see a real data flywheel.

And third, the form factor matters. The world is designed for the human body: our kitchens, factories, tools, door handles. If you can get a general-purpose humanoid cheap enough, you don't have to redesign the environment for each task. One hardware platform, one foundation model, many tasks. That's the bet.

So it's not that cheap hardware solves robotics on its own. The hard part is still the brain, the foundation model for physical AI. But cheap hardware removes a bottleneck that held the field back for decades. It's a bit like GPUs becoming accessible before deep learning took off. The pieces are lining up, and that's why I think this time feels different.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I get really excited about. If you look at the hardware side of humanoid robotics, we're basically seeing a Moore's Law type of curve, except it's happening a lot faster than anyone expected. A few years ago, a research-grade humanoid would cost you a few hundred thousand dollars, maybe more. Now you have companies, especially out of China, shipping full humanoids in the tens of thousands of dollars range, and some of the smaller form factors are even cheaper than that. That's roughly the price of a car. And once you're in car territory, the economics of this whole field change.

The reason that matters so much for someone like me, who works on the AI side, is that hardware was always the bottleneck for data. In language, we had the internet. We had trillions of tokens just sitting there for free. Robotics never had that. There is no internet of robot actions. Every data point has to be physically collected by a robot moving in the real world, or generated in simulation. So if a robot costs half a million dollars, you can afford maybe a handful in your lab, and your data collection is tiny. If a robot costs twenty thousand, you can have a fleet. A university can have a fleet. A startup can have a fleet. Suddenly you're collecting orders of magnitude more real-world data, and that's the fuel that these foundation models need.

The other piece is that the price drop is a signal about the supply chain. It means the actuators, the sensors, the batteries, the hands are all becoming commodities. Hands in particular used to be this exotic, artisanal thing. Now you can buy a dexterous hand off the shelf. And when hardware commoditizes, the differentiation moves up the stack into software, into the brain. That's exactly the world I want to be in, because the brain is where the general-purpose intelligence lives, and that's where you can get something like a GPT moment for robotics.

And I'd add one more thing. Humanoids specifically benefit from this because the form factor is designed for a world built by humans, for humans. Doors, stairs, tools, kitchens. So the training data we collect, including from human video, transfers more naturally. Cheap humanoid hardware plus a general robot foundation model plus simulation at scale. Those three things are converging right now, and that's why I'm more optimistic than I've ever been.

astra-6.text:
Because it changes who gets to experiment. When a humanoid costs as much as a luxury car, very few labs can afford a fleet. As prices come down, more researchers and developers can get their hands on one, try ideas, break things, and learn. That can accelerate progress enormously.

And there’s a feedback loop: cheaper robots mean more deployments, more deployments give us more data about what works and what fails, and that data helps us build better robot intelligence. Hardware becoming accessible doesn’t solve the intelligence problem, but it gives us many more opportunities to solve it. That’s why I find the price trend so encouraging.

sol-6.1.text:
The exciting thing is that cheaper hardware changes who gets to experiment. When a humanoid costs hundreds of thousands of dollars, only a handful of labs can afford one, and every experiment is precious. As that price comes down, more researchers and developers can get their hands on robots, try ideas, and learn from failures.

That matters because robotics needs a lot of interaction with the real world. Affordable robots let us collect more data and test across more environments. Better software can then make those robots more useful, which creates demand and helps bring costs down further.

Price alone doesn’t solve the intelligence problem. But it lowers the barrier to working on it, and that’s a very powerful reason for optimism.
